title: Coloring A Border
prompt: You are given an `m x n` integer matrix `grid`, and three integers `row`, `col`, and `color`. The grid represents a board where `grid[i][j]` is the color of cell `(i, j)`. Two cells belong to the same connected component if they have the same color and are 4-directionally adjacent. The border of a connected component is the set of cells in that component that are either on the edge of the grid, or adjacent to a cell not in the component (different color). Find the connected component containing `(row, col)`, color all its border cells with `color`, and return the final grid. Note: the newly assigned `color` may equal an existing color in the grid.

examples.explanation: The component of 1s containing (0,0) is {(0,0),(0,1),(1,0)}; all three cells are on the border, so all become 3.
The component of 2s containing (0,1) has every one of its cells on the border, so they're all recolored; the interior 3 at (1,1) is a different component and untouched.
The single interior cell (1,1) is the only cell in the component not adjacent to the grid edge or a different color, so it alone stays uncolored while every surrounding cell becomes the border.

hints: First find the entire connected component containing (row, col) using DFS or BFS, exactly like flood fill, tracking which cells belong to it.

A cell in the component is a border cell if it's on the edge of the grid, OR any of its 4 neighbors is in bounds but belongs to a different component (different original color, or already visited-and-different).

Do the border check using the ORIGINAL colors (or a separate visited marker), and only overwrite cells to the new color after you've identified the full component and its borders — otherwise overwriting mid-traversal can make same-component cells look like a different color to their neighbors.

solution.approach: DFS from (row, col), tracking visited cells belonging to the target component using the original color (captured before any mutation). While visiting each cell, check whether it's a border cell: either it's on the grid's edge, or it has a neighbor that is in bounds but not part of the same component (different original color or a cell not visited during this DFS). Collect border cells separately and only overwrite them to the new color after the full DFS finishes, so the component-membership test isn't corrupted by partial recoloring during the walk.
